specPoints.text: understand how ions are formed by electron loss or gain

primer.text: Atomic structure is old ground: protons and electrons counted, shells filled two-eight-eight. This note puts that picture to work - when atoms give up or take in electrons to reach a full outer shell, the balance between protons and electrons tips and charged particles called ions appear.

lessons.title: Formation of Ions
lessons.opening: When an atom loses or gains electrons it stops being neutral and becomes an ion - a charged particle. Atoms make this trade to reach a full outer shell, the stable arrangement the noble gases already hold. Lose electrons and the charge is positive; gain them and it is negative.
keyPoints: An ion is an atom or group of atoms that carries an electric charge after losing or gaining electrons.
The loss or gain of electrons happens so the atom can reach a full outer shell.
Ions of group 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 elements end with a noble gas electronic structure.
The noble gases named in the note are helium, neon and argon.
Every metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positive ion; every non-metal gains electrons and becomes a negative ion.

low.restatement: Ions form when atoms give up or take in electrons, and the charge tells which way it went: positive for lost, negative for gained. Groups 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 all land on a noble gas arrangement.
low.analogy: Think of a supermarket loyalty card: a shopper one sticker short of a free item grabs one more, while a shopper holding one too many hands it back. Atoms gain or shed electrons the same way to reach a full card - a full outer shell.
low.examPointer: Exam questions ask why ions carry their charges: the answer is electron loss or gain, never proton changes - the nucleus never moves.

medium.restatement: The definition has two halves: the particle, one atom or a group of atoms, and the charge, set by electrons lost or gained. Reaching a full outer shell is the driver, which is why group membership predicts the charge before any formula work starts.
medium.analogy: A full bus already moving is like a noble gas atom - complete, so it does not bother changing. Atoms short of a full bus squeeze on, atoms with spare passengers step off; either way the journey ends with a complete shell.
medium.examPointer: The note's exam hint is worth memorising: electrons gained or lost equal the charge, so 2 electrons lost means 2+, and 1 electron gained means 1-.

options.text: An atom or group of atoms that carries an electric charge
options.explanation: Losing or gaining electrons leaves the particle charged; that charged particle is the ion.

options.text: An atom that has gained or lost protons
options.explanation: Protons stay fixed in the nucleus; ions differ only in their electrons.

options.text: An atom with extra neutrons
options.explanation: Neutron changes make isotopes, not ions - a different idea entirely.

options.text: Any atom with a full outer shell
options.explanation: Noble gases have full shells but no charge; charge, not fullness, makes the ion.

check.stem: Why do atoms lose or gain electrons?

options.text: To reach a full outer shell of electrons
options.explanation: The full outer shell is the stable target; the charge is the side effect.

options.text: To turn into a noble gas element
options.explanation: The electronic structure matches a noble gas, but the particle stays the same element.

options.text: To balance the protons in the nucleus
options.explanation: The proton count never changes during ion forming.

options.text: To become electrically neutral
options.explanation: Neutral is the starting point; the whole point of the trade is ending up charged.

check.stem: A sodium atom loses its single outer electron. Which noble gas does its electronic structure then match?

options.text: Neon
options.explanation: Sodium at 2,8,1 drops to 2,8 - neon's own arrangement.

options.text: Helium
options.explanation: Helium holds only 2 electrons; sodium's ion keeps two full shells beneath.

options.text: Argon
options.explanation: Argon sits at 2,8,8; sodium's ion has one shell fewer than that.

options.text: Krypton
options.explanation: Krypton is two shells larger still; nothing in sodium's loss reaches it.

check.stem: Which statement covers every metal and every non-metal in ion forming?

options.text: All metals lose electrons; all non-metals gain them
options.explanation: The note states the rule without exceptions: metals lose, non-metals gain.

options.text: Metals gain and non-metals lose
options.explanation: Backwards - the losing side is always the metal.

options.text: Both lose electrons at the same time
options.explanation: If both lost, neither could accept; the exchange needs one giver and one taker.

options.text: Only some metals take part
options.explanation: The rule is all metals - there are no bystander metals here.

check.stem: How does the charge of an ion relate to the electrons moved?

options.text: The charge equals the number of electrons gained or lost
options.explanation: Two electrons lost gives 2+, and 1 electron gained gives 1- - the count and the charge always match.

options.text: The charge equals the outer-shell total
options.explanation: The outer-shell total sets how many move, not the charge itself.

options.text: The charge is always 1, whatever moves
options.explanation: Charges of 2+ and 3- exist wherever two or three electrons move.

options.text: The charge equals the proton count
options.explanation: Protons fix the element, not the ion's charge; electrons decide the charge.

check.stem: Name the three noble gases the note names for electronic structures.
State what every metal atom does in ion forming, and what every non-metal atom does.
check.modelAnswer: Every metal atom loses electrons and becomes a positive ion; every non-metal gains electrons and becomes a negative ion.

check.stem: Explain why an atom that gives up electrons ends up with a positive charge.
check.modelAnswer: Because electrons are negative — losing them leaves more protons than electrons, so the particle's overall charge is positive.

check.stem: An oxygen atom has 8 electrons (2,6) and gains 2 more. State the ion's charge and the noble-gas structure it now matches.
check.modelAnswer: The ion carries a 2- charge and matches the 2,8 structure of neon.

lessons.title: Formation of Cations and Anions
lessons.opening: Two names sort the charged particles: cations are positive ions born from lost electrons, anions are negative ions built from gained ones. Metals always lose, non-metals always gain. The diagrams trace sodium dropping one electron to become Na+, and chlorine picking one up to become Cl-.
keyPoints: Cations are positive ions that form when atoms lose electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.
Anions are negative ions that form when atoms gain electrons, ending with more electrons than protons.
Every metal sheds electrons to other atoms and turns into a positive ion.
Every non-metal takes electrons from other atoms and turns into a negative ion.
A magnesium atom that loses 2 electrons carries a 2+ charge; a bromine atom that gains 1 electron carries a 1- charge.

low.restatement: Cations and anions are the two names to keep straight: cations lost electrons and read positive, anions gained electrons and read negative. Metals feed one side, non-metals the other, and the note's diagrams show sodium and chlorine each taking their route.
low.analogy: Paying for a bus fare works both ways: hand over coins and you are short, take coins in and you are carrying extra. Electrons are the currency - paying them out charges the ion positive, collecting them charges it negative.
low.examPointer: Charge questions answer themselves once the count is known: magnesium losing 2 electrons reads 2+, bromine gaining 1 electron reads 1-.

medium.restatement: The pairing is symmetrical: a cation has more protons than electrons because electrons left, and an anion has more electrons than protons because electrons arrived. The sodium and chloride diagrams mirror each other - one electron out for the metal, one electron in for the non-metal.
medium.analogy: Two shop tills face each other at closing: one till pays out and its balance runs positive on the ledger of lost coins, the other takes in and runs negative. Metals pay electrons out, non-metals take them in, and the charge records the direction.
medium.examPointer: Diagram questions expect the charge arrow as well as the movement: Na+ and Cl- must carry their signs, and the exam hint's count rule justifies each one.

options.text: A negative ion with more electrons than protons
options.explanation: Gaining electrons tips the balance negative; the extra electrons make the anion.

options.text: A positive ion with more protons than electrons
options.explanation: That describes a cation - the name swap catches learners who mix the two labels.

options.text: An atom that has gained protons
options.explanation: Protons never transfer between atoms; only electrons move when ions form.

options.text: A neutral atom with a full outer shell
options.explanation: A full outer shell often follows ion forming, but the particle is charged, not neutral.

check.stem: What happens to metal atoms when they take part in ion forming?

options.text: They lose electrons and become positive ions
options.explanation: Every metal loses electrons; shedding them leaves more protons than electrons.

options.text: They gain electrons and become negative ions
options.explanation: That is the non-metal route; metals sit on the losing side.

options.text: They share electrons with non-metals
options.explanation: Sharing belongs to covalent bonding, a different subtopic.

options.text: They stay neutral because metals are stable
options.explanation: Metals do not keep their outer electrons; they hand them over and charge up.

check.stem: A magnesium atom loses 2 electrons. What charge does the ion carry?

options.explanation: Each lost electron adds one positive unit: two electrons lost, so 2+.
The negative sign belongs to gains; losing electrons cannot leave a negative charge.
The count is two lost electrons, not one; the charge counts every electron moved.
Losing electrons always leaves a charge; neutrality belonged to the atom before the loss.

check.stem: A bromine atom gains 1 electron. What charge does the ion carry?

options.explanation: One extra electron means one negative unit, so the ion is 1-.
Gains make negative ions; a positive sign would mean a loss.
Seven is the outer-shell count, not the charge; only gained electrons count.
The gained electron changes the balance; the ion cannot stay neutral.

check.stem: In the note's chloride diagram, what does the chlorine atom do to reach a full outer shell?

options.text: It gains 1 electron and becomes Cl-
options.explanation: Non-metals gain; one electron in gives the chloride ion its 1- charge.

options.text: It loses 1 electron and becomes Cl+
options.explanation: Losing is the metal behaviour; chlorine takes the gaining route.
options.misconception: metal behaviour applied to a non-metal

options.text: It gains 7 electrons
options.explanation: Filling the shell needs one electron, not seven; the last shell is one short.

options.text: It loses its whole outer shell
options.explanation: Shells are not discarded; electrons are transferred one or two at a time.

check.modelAnswer: A cation is a positive ion that forms when an atom loses electrons, leaving more protons than electrons.

check.stem: State the charge on the magnesium ion and on the bromide ion from the lesson's examples.
check.modelAnswer: Magnesium loses 2 electrons for a 2+ charge; bromine gains 1 electron for a 1- charge.

check.stem: Explain why an anion carries a negative charge.
check.modelAnswer: Because gaining electrons leaves more electrons than protons, so the overall charge is negative.

check.stem: Aluminium (Group 3) reacts with sulfur (Group 6). State which element forms the cation, which forms the anion, and each ion's charge.
check.modelAnswer: Aluminium is the cation at 3+ (a Group 3 metal donating its three outer electrons); sulfur is the anion at 2- (a Group 6 non-metal receiving two electrons).

glossary.definition: An atom or group of atoms that carries an electric charge after losing or gaining electrons.
The complete outermost electron shell that atoms chase when they lose or gain electrons.
One of the unreactive elements with a full outer shell already in place - helium, neon and argon are the named examples.
The arrangement of electrons across an atom's shells.
The sign and size of the imbalance left when electrons are gained or lost, quoted as 1-, 2+ and so on.
A positive ion, formed when an atom loses electrons.
A negative ion, formed when an atom gains electrons.

workedExample.prompt: a) A magnesium atom loses 2 electrons. State the charge of the ion formed and the name for this type of ion. b) A bromine atom gains 1 electron. State the charge and the ion type. c) Explain why ions of Group 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 elements have a noble-gas electronic structure.
steps: a) The number of electrons lost equals the charge, so losing 2 electrons gives a Mg2+ ion — a cation, the name for a positive ion formed by electron loss.
b) Gaining 1 electron gives a 1- charge, so the ion is Br- — an anion, the name for a negative ion formed by electron gain.

c) Atoms lose or gain electrons precisely to obtain a full outer shell, which is the arrangement noble gases such as helium, neon and argon already hold; ions of these groups therefore finish with a noble-gas electronic structure.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Mg2+, a cation. b) Br-, an anion. c) The electron loss or gain happens to reach a full outer shell — the noble-gas configuration.
